body.heading: Light, lit on purpose
paragraphs: In the darkest part of the year, many cultures independently arrive at the same answer: make light yourselves. Diwali fills homes and streets with oil lamps and candles, celebrating light's victory over darkness and good over evil. Hanukkah adds one candle each night for eight nights, remembering a small jar of oil that burned far longer than it should have.

Sweden's St Lucia day brings a procession led by a girl in white wearing a crown of candles, carrying light — and saffron buns — into the December dark. China's Lantern Festival closes the New Year celebrations with streets full of lanterns, riddles written on them for passers-by to solve.

body.heading: Different stories, one gesture
paragraphs: The theologies differ; the gesture is shared. A small flame, lit deliberately, in company, when the world is at its darkest. Children understand these festivals instantly because the symbolism needs no translation: it is dark, we are together, look — a light.

Food follows the light: sweets at Diwali, fried foods at Hanukkah recalling the oil, sweet rice dumplings at the Lantern Festival symbolising family wholeness. Celebration you can eat is a feature of nearly every festival humans keep.

body.heading: Your own darkest-week ritual
paragraphs: Any family can honour the pattern: choose one evening in the darkest week, eat by candlelight, and let each person name one light of their year — a person, a moment, a kindness. It borrows the gesture, respectfully, and makes it yours.

Blow the candles out one by one at the end, naming nothing, just noticing the dark return and the company still there. Then put the lights back on and have pudding. Festivals end with food for a reason.

description: Diwali lamps, Hanukkah candles, St Lucia's crown, and streets of lanterns: in the darkest months, cultures everywhere make light on purpose.
